title: The Phantom of the Opera

subtitle.text: As the dancers made their way to the ballet foyer, they discussed the horrible death of Buquet.
On the stairs Mercier, the managers' assistant, stopped them when he overheard their conversation.
"Have you girls heard about Buquet already? Most people haven't, so please forget about it for tonight."
He waggled a finger at them. "And don't let Monsieur Debienne and Monsieur Poligny hear.
It would upset the managers too much on their last night at the opera house."
By the time the dancers reached the foyer, it was already full of people.
Everyone was talking about the amazing performance they'd just witnessed.
Many of the great composers of the day had appeared onstage, conducting their own works.
But the real star was the young singer Christine Daaé.
She'd begun with a few selections from [i@Romeo and Juliet@i] and concluded by singing the leading role of Marguerite in some excerpts from [i@Faust@i].
Carlotta, a famous Spanish diva, usually sang Marguerite, but she was ill that night.
So Christine, who usually portrayed a boy in [i@Faust@i], had taken her place.
And what a magnificent performance she'd given!
The whole audience had risen to its feet, shouting, cheering, clapping, while a sobbing Christine was overcome by the response.
She'd fainted in the arms of other singers and been carried to her dressing room.
Everyone in the foyer wanted to know why Christine hadn't appeared in a leading role before this performance.
Even more mysterious was the rumor that she didn't have a voice coach.
"I hear she plans to keep rehearsing on her own with no intention of finding a coach," one audience member confided to another.
"Well, whatever she's doing, it's working. I attended one of her performances six months ago, and the difference between then and now . . ."
The other man paused. "It's unbelievable."
Philippe, the Count de Chagny, should have been in the foyer, supporting his favorite dancer, Sorelli, as she gave her speech to the managers.
Instead he was following his much younger brother, Raoul, the Viscount de Chagny, through the maze of passages that led to Christine's dressing room.
"Why are you in such a hurry?" Philippe asked his brother.
"Didn't you see that poor woman faint? I must make sure she's all right!"
Philippe smiled at his younger brother's urgent tone. Raoul was only 21, and obviously infatuated with the lovely young Christine.
The two brothers forced their way through a crowd of singers and fans gathered outside Christine's dressing room.
They reached her door just as the theater's doctor was arriving. Raoul rushed to the unconscious singer's side while Philippe and the others pushed into the room.
"Everyone should clear the room," Raoul said to the doctor. "There's no space to breathe in here."
"You're quite right." The doctor sent everyone away except Christine's maid and Raoul.
Christine's eyelashes fluttered as she regained consciousness.
Turning her head, she spotted Raoul at her side and started. "Monsieur," she said in a barely audible voice, "who are you?"
"Mademoiselle . . ." Raoul knelt on one knee and kissed her hand.
"I'm the boy who went into the sea to rescue your scarf."
Christine looked nervously at the doctor and her maid, trying to gauge what they thought of Raoul's odd remark.
When they laughed, Christine joined in, though she still looked uneasy.
Raoul turned red with embarrassment and stood up. "Mademoiselle, since you don't seem to recognize me, I'd like to say something to you in private. Something very important."
Christine's voice shook. "You must wait until I am better."
The doctor nodded. "Please go now and let me attend to mademoiselle."
"Thank you, doctor, but I would like to be alone." Christine looked nervously around the room. "Please go away, all of you."
The doctor tried to protest, but observing Christine's agitation, he escorted Raoul from the room.
"She's not her usual self; she's usually so gentle," the doctor said.
He bid Raoul good night and left him in the now deserted passage.
Raoul thought Christine might attend the farewell ceremony in the ballet foyer, so he lingered in the shadows near her doorway.
Soon the dressing room door opened, and her maid came out, carrying a bundle of laundry.
"Excuse me, how is she?" Raoul asked.
"She's quite well, but you must not disturb her because she wants to be alone. Good night, sir." The maid hurried away.
"Of course Christine told her maid that she wants to be alone," Raoul said to himself.
"That's because she's waiting for me. She knows I want to speak to her in private."
Raoul was about to knock on the door when he heard a man's voice inside the room.
"Christine, do you love me?" the man said.
"How can you ask that when I sing only for you?" Christine sounded sad and on the verge of tears.
Raoul's heart was pounding so loudly that he was sure Christine and the man could hear it.
The man spoke again. "Are you very tired, my dear?"
"Yes, I gave you my soul tonight, and I'm dead tired."
"Your soul is a beautiful thing, and I thank you. No emperor ever received so rare a gift."
Overcome with jealousy, Raoul heard nothing after that.
But he now understood why Christine was so nervous: she was expecting this visitor.
Raoul returned to the shadows, determined to wait for the man to leave the room.
To his surprise, Christine appeared first, and she was alone.
Raoul was still too rattled by what he'd overheard to approach her.
He waited a few minutes before opening the door to her dressing room and found himself in complete darkness because the gaslights had been turned off.
"I know someone's in here," Raoul said with his back against the door. "Why are you hiding?"
He lit the gas and searched behind the curtain that divided the room, but no one was there.
"I must be going mad!" he thought.
Raoul left the room in a daze. At the bottom of a staircase he felt an icy draft.
Suddenly two men were behind him, carrying something under a white sheet.
"Excuse me," Raoul said. "Can you tell me the way out?"
"The door's open straight ahead," one man grunted.
"Thank you. What's that you're carrying?"
"That is Joseph Buquet, the chief stagehand, whose body was found tonight in the third cellar beneath the stage," the man explained.
Raoul removed his hat as a mark of respect for the dead and let the men pass.
After a few days, the new managers forgot about the ghost—until they received an envelope addressed in red ink.
Richard opened the letter and read it aloud to his partner, Moncharmin.
[i@Dear Sirs:
I am sorry to bother you when you must be busy reviewing the singers' and dancers' contracts, deciding whom to keep and whom to fire.
I assume you realize that Carlotta's voice is nothing compared to Christine's.
So I fail to understand why Christine has not been allowed to play the part of Marguerite in Faust since her triumph at the gala.
However, I would still like to hear her tonight, when she'll perform her usual role of the boy Siébel.
Therefore I ask you not to sell my box tonight or any other night.@i]
[i@Several times when I've arrived at the opera, I have been disagreeably surprised to find that my box has been sold.
I did not protest because I dislike scandal and also because I thought your predecessors had failed to mention my request.
I wrote to them and have now received a reply, which proves that you are treating me with outrageous contempt. Please see the enclosed newspaper clipping.
If you wish to live in peace, you must never take away my private box!
Sincerely yours,
The Opera Ghost@i]
The letter was accompanied by a personal ad cut from the newspaper:
[i@OG: There is no excuse for R & M's behavior. We showed them your additions in the book.
—D & P@i]
Richard shook his head in disbelief. "Debienne and Poligny are still carrying on with their joke.
They even went to the expense of putting an ad in the newspaper!"
"They're harmless enough," Moncharmin said, "but what do they really want? A box for tonight's performance?"
"Perhaps we should send them tickets for box five, if it's not already sold," Richard said.
Moncharmin nodded. The two managers spent the rest of the day and evening negotiating contracts.
Exhausted, they left the opera house without checking if their predecessors were enjoying the performance.
The next morning they received a note from the opera ghost:
[i@Dear Sirs:
Thank you. Charming evening. Will soon write about arrangements for your first payment of 20,000 francs.
Kind regards,
OG@i]
"This is outrageous!" Moncharmin said. "And look, here's a ridiculous reply from Debienne and Poligny.
Apparently they didn't even come to the opera last night!"
[i@Gentlemen:
We are much obliged to you for thinking of us, but we cannot use tickets to box five.
As we have explained, that box is exclusively reserved for the person whom we have discussed with you.
Most sincerely,
Debienne and Poligny@i]
Richard ripped up both notes and tossed them into a wastebasket.
"These fellows are beginning to annoy me! As of tonight, we're selling box five's seats to anyone who wants them!"
The following morning the managers found a security guard's report in their office.
"There was some trouble with box five last night," Moncharmin said, summarizing the report for Richard.
"The ticket holders didn't arrive until the beginning of the second act. The moment they entered the box, a voice said that the seats were taken.
They saw no one, so they came out and called the usher, who checked the box and found it empty.
When the patrons reentered the box, they heard the voice again.
They consulted the usher, who said it must be the opera ghost.
At which point, the ticket holders became loud and abusive, and the usher called the security guard, who removed them."
"We need to speak to that usher right now!" Richard said.
Moments later the usher, a woman in a black dress and faded shawl, entered the office.
"What's your name?" Richard asked.
"Madame Giry. I'm the mother of Meg, one of your best dancers," she said with obvious pride.
"Never heard of her," Richard said. "Tell us what happened last night with box five."
"I was planning to talk to you about box five, so you wouldn't have the same trouble as Monsieur Debienne and Monsieur Poligny.
They wouldn't listen to me at first, and—"
"Never mind that," Richard interrupted. "I'm asking what happened last night."
Madame Giry turned purple with indignation because no one had ever spoken to her like that.
She replied in a haughty voice. "I'll tell you what happened. The ghost was annoyed again!"
"The ghost! Don't talk to me about that—"
"Calm yourself, Richard," Moncharmin said, "and let me take over here."
He turned to the usher and politely said, "Now, madame, tell us all about your ghost in box five."
Madame Giry nodded. "No one ever sees him, but everybody can hear him.
I've often heard him, and you can believe me because I always tell the truth."
Behind her back, Richard gave his partner a skeptical look, but Moncharmin persisted.
"Have you ever spoken to the ghost, my good lady?"
"Oh, yes! Just like I'm speaking to you now, sir."
"And when the ghost speaks to you, what does he say?" Moncharmin asked.
"He usually asks me to bring him a program."
Richard snorted. "A program?"
"Well, I can't very well hand it to him when he arrives, can I?" Madame Giry glared at Richard. "I never see him arrive."
"How do you know the ghost is a man?" Moncharmin asked.
"He has a man's voice, such a lovely voice." Madame Giry clasped her hands together in delight.
"When he arrives, it's usually in the middle of the first act.
He gives three little taps on the door of box five.
The first time I heard that tapping, I was puzzled because I knew there was no one in the box.
I opened the door, and the voice requested a program."
"And how did you react?"
"Well, I wasn't afraid even though the voice said it was the opera ghost.
It spoke to me so kindly and mentioned my dear, departed husband."
"Did you see the ghost leave the box?" Moncharmin said.
"No, but after the performance, the program was gone, and the ghost had left me a tip."
"A tip?" Richard rolled his eyes because her story was becoming more unbelievable every minute.
"Yes, a tip," Madame Giry insisted. "Usually he leaves just a few francs, but once he left a box of English candy, which I'm very fond of.
However, now that people are annoying him again, he leaves me nothing."
"Thank you, that will do," Moncharmin said, indicating the door.
As soon as Madame Giry had left, the managers agreed to fire her and investigate box five themselves.
Fearing that his lantern might cause the barrel of gunpowder to explode, the Persian tossed it aside.
It broke, leaving the Persian and Raoul in the dark.
They couldn't even rely on the light shining through the open trapdoor because it had been switched off.
"We must return to the hexagon room and try to speak with Christine." The Persian stumbled against a barrel.
"With our discovery of the gunpowder, I finally understand Erik's threat.
If Christine doesn't agree to marry him, he'll blow up the opera house at eleven o'clock tomorrow night!"
Raoul was stunned. "At that hour the opera house will be full of people! But Christine will never agree to spend the rest of her life with such a monster."
"I don't think she realizes the life-or-death consequences of her decision," the Persian said as they carefully climbed the stairs to the hexagon room.
"Eleven o'clock tomorrow night." Raoul repeated as the two men sat on the floor in total darkness.
"I wonder what time it is," the Persian said. "My watch has stopped."
"It seems like we've been stuck in this mirrored prison for years," Raoul put his watch up to his ear.
"Mine is still ticking, but I can't see the hands to tell the time."
"Break the glass and touch the hands."
Raoul did as he was told. "Judging by the space between the hands, I'd say it's almost 11 o'clock."
"But is that morning or the evening?"
"I don't know! Who could keep track of time when we were in the forest? Or in the desert?"
Raoul's voice grew louder as he became more frustrated.
"We may have 12 hours until Erik's explosion or only a few minutes. I have no idea."
"Hush!" the Persian said. "I hear footsteps coming from Christine's room next door."
"Raoul, Raoul!" Christine said. "Is that you I hear? Are you still alive?"
"Yes, my darling."
"Oh, thank goodness." Christine began to sob with relief.
"I promised to marry Erik if he took me to the hexagon room, but he refused. He said there was no more need for that key and threw it in the lake.
He's gone out for a few minutes to give me time to decide whether to marry him or not. Oh, Raoul, I thought you were dead. I thought—"
"Mademoiselle! What time is it?" the Persian interrupted.
"Five minutes before 11."
"Yes, but in the morning or the evening?"
"The evening. It's five minutes before I must make my decision.
Oh, Raoul, I'm so frightened. Erik tore off his mask, and his eyes shot yellow flames.
Then he handed me the other key from his leather bag—the brass one—and said it opens both ebony boxes on my mantel.
He called it the key of life or death. I don't understand why he said that, but—"
"It must have something to do with the gunpowder," the Persian said.
"Gunpowder?" Christine paused. "Erik didn't say anything about gunpowder.
He said one box contained a brass scorpion and the other a brass grasshopper.
If I turned the scorpion around, that meant I'd marry him. But if I turned the grasshopper, that meant my answer was no.
His last words were 'Be careful of the grasshopper. It hops! It hops really high!'"
"You know Erik," Raoul said to the Persian. "What do you think he means about the grasshopper hopping really high?"
"I have no doubt that the grasshopper controls an electric current that will blow up the barrels of gunpowder."
"Why do you keep talking about gunpowder?" Christine asked.
Raoul quickly explained the situation to his fiancée and urged her to turn the scorpion at once.
"No! Don't touch the scorpion!" the Persian cried.
"What?" Raoul said.
"This may be another trick of Erik's," the Persian said. "He couldn't really expect Christine to marry him, so perhaps he gave her the wrong information.
Maybe he's hiding somewhere, waiting to watch the opera house explode from a safe distance."
"Here he comes!" Christine said.
The two men heard Erik's footsteps as he entered the room next door.
"Hello, Erik!" the Persian called out boldly.
With extraordinary calmness, Erik replied, "So you're not dead in there."
The Persian tried to reply, but Erik silenced him. "Not a word or I shall blow up everything, and that honor belongs to Mademoiselle Christine.
I see that she has not touched the scorpion or the grasshopper, but it's not too late to do the right thing. Give me the key, my dear."
Erik laughed wickedly and opened the two boxes for Christine.

"Let's look at both creatures, shall we? Aren't they pretty? If you choose the grasshopper, we shall all be blown up because there is enough gunpowder under our feet to destroy the whole neighborhood.
But if you choose the scorpion, the gunpowder will be soaked with water and made useless.
All those Parisians upstairs listening to a second-rate opera will be forever grateful to you for saving their lives. And we shall be happily married!"
Erik paused. "If you haven't turned the scorpion in two minutes, I will turn the grasshopper."
There was a long, terrible silence during which Raoul prayed and the Persian listened to his heart pounding.
"Your two minutes are up," Erik announced. "Good-bye, Christine. Hop, grasshopper!"
"Wait!" Christine cried. "Do you promise that the scorpion is the right one to turn?"
"Yes, but if you won't turn it now, I'll turn the grasshopper."
"Erik!"
"Enough!" Erik roared.
"Erik! I've turned the scorpion!"
The Persian and Raoul heard a hissing noise beneath their feet as water flowed into the room below them.
They had forgotten their thirst, but now they ran to the bottom of the steps and drank and drank.
As the water rose, they retreated up the staircase, step by step.
The water came out of the cellar and flooded the floor of the hexagon room.
"Erik, that's enough water. The gunpowder is soaked," the Persian called out. "Turn off the tap."
"Christine, the water is up to our knees!" Raoul said.
But Erik did not reply and neither did Christine.
The Persian and Raoul were alone in the dark with the water rising and no one to turn off the tap.
They lost their footing and were thrown against the mirrors as the water spun them around the hexagon room.
"I love you, Christine!" Raoul called.
"Erik, remember that I saved your life!" the Persian cried, but it was too late. The water filled the room, and the two men lost consciousness.
When the Persian regained consciousness, he was lying in bed, and Raoul was nearby, asleep on a sofa.
An angel and a devil—Christine and Erik—were watching over them.
The Persian raised himself on one elbow and looked around the room. "Where are we?"
"You're in Christine's room in my house," Erik replied.
"As is the viscount. He woke up long before we knew if you were still alive, but we must let him sleep now.
Soon I will take you up to the surface of the earth to please my wife."
The Persian was startled by those last words, but they had no effect on Christine, who sat quietly reading.
Erik gave the Persian something to drink and warned him not to speak to Christine or Raoul. The next thing the Persian knew, he was waking up in his own bed at home.
"How did I get here?" the Persian asked his servant, Darius, who was standing by the bed.
"Someone rang the doorbell last night, sir," Darius said. "When I answered the door, you were the only person there, and you were unconscious."
Hoping that Raoul had also been brought home, the Persian sent a message to his house.
But the reply that came back was upsetting: Raoul was missing, and his brother, Philippe, was dead.
The count's body had been found on the edge of the lake underneath the opera house.
"How terrible!" the Persian muttered, rereading the note.
From what he knew about Erik and things Raoul had told him, he pieced together what had happened.
When Philippe thought Christine and Raoul had eloped, he went after them.
Failing to find them, Philippe had dashed back into the opera house and entered the cellars, where he became the siren's victim.
The Persian shuddered, remembering Erik's playing of the funeral mass.
He rang for his servant. "Darius, help me get dressed, and then summon a cab. I must go to the police at once."
But the police did not take the Persian's evidence seriously. A murderer and kidnapper was living by the lake under the opera house? How was that possible?
And so the Persian returned home, determined to write down his story and hand it to the newspapers.
While he was writing, a mysterious man appeared at his apartment, demanding to see him.
"The stranger won't tell me his name or show his face," Darius reported to the Persian. "He refuses to leave until he has spoken to you."
"Send him in," the Persian said to his servant. "I know who it is."
The Persian rose to his feet as Erik entered his drawing room. Erik looked extremely weak and leaned against the wall as if he was afraid of falling.
"Murderer of Count Philippe, what have you done with Raoul and Christine?" the Persian demanded.
Erik staggered under this direct attack and dragged himself to a chair.
"Don't talk to me about Philippe. The siren caused him to have an unfortunate accident, and he fell into the lake."
"Liar!" the Persian shouted.
Erik bowed his head. "I haven't come here to talk about Philippe, but to tell you that I'm dying. I'm—"
"Where are Christine and Raoul?"
Erik ignored the Persian's question and went on, gasping for breath.
"I'm dying of love. I've always loved Christine, and I love her now more than ever.
You should have heard how she begged me to release you and Raoul. She promised to marry me if I spared your lives, so I carried you here."
"Answer me!" the Persian shouted. "Are Christine and Raoul alive?"
"Of course they are. After I took you home, I chained Raoul in a dungeon under the opera house. And then . . ."
Erik was momentarily overcome with emotion. "And then Christine let me kiss her on the forehead!
You can't imagine what that was like for me. My poor, unhappy mother would never let me kiss her. She used to toss me my mask and run away.
Nor has any other woman ever allowed me to kiss her. I was so happy that I cried and fell at Christine's feet.
And when I looked up, Christine was crying too!"
As the Persian watched Erik sob, tears of pity came to his own eyes.
"He's committed some terrible crimes," the Persian thought, "but what a sad, unfortunate man."
Erik took a deep breath and began again. "When I felt Christine's tears on my forehead, I removed my mask so I wouldn't lose a single one of her tears.
And she didn't run away! She stayed with me, weeping over me, weeping with me.
At that moment I felt all the happiness the world had to offer."
Erik began coughing and sputtering. "I heard Christine say, 'Poor, unhappy Erik!' and she took my hand.
I had found the gold ring that she'd lost after I'd given it to her.
I slipped the ring on her hand and told her to take it for herself and for Raoul.
When she asked what I meant, I told her I was releasing her from her promise to marry me.
She could marry Raoul whenever she wanted because she had cried with me."
At that point Erik told the Persian not to look at him. "I have to remove my mask because I'm choking."
The Persian walked over to the window and opened it. His heart was full of pity, but he kept his eyes on the scene outside his window.
When he heard Erik take a deep breath and put the mask back on, he turned around and found Erik ready to continue talking.
"I immediately brought Raoul to Christine, and they kissed in front of me.
I made Christine promise to wear my ring until she learned of my death, when she should go to my house and bury the ring with my body.
Then Christine kissed me right here!"
Erik tapped his forehead.
"She and Raoul hurried off together, making plans for their wedding, and leaving me—the only person still crying—alone."
The Persian was no longer worried about Christine and Raoul because he had no doubt that Erik was telling the truth.
He had no further questions for Erik, who rose to leave.
"I do have one final request," Erik said at the door.
"When I feel the end is near, I will notify you. Then you must put an ad in the newspaper so the young couple will know that I have died."
Three weeks later an ad appeared in one of the Paris newspapers: "Erik is dead."
